chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara war reaches its height: armies of elephants, chariots and archers clash, the hero's arrows blind and rout the foe, and the proud rival king, told his army has broken, answers with a laugh.

cast.role: the Vidyadharas of the rival host, who are routed
the young king of the southern mountain, who joins the battle
the staff-bearing man who reports the broken army to the king
the proud king whose army has broken; read as Acuvakanthan
the earth's kings who laugh and who are ashamed to retreat

1231.reading: The host comes down on the wedding city like clouds rising and spreading into a great sea, swordsmen and bowmen darkening all eight quarters.
1231.nuance: The verse does not say whose host it is; reading it as the Vidyadhara host of the rival king rests on the story so far.
1231.event: A sword- and bow-bearing host descends on the city and darkens the sky.

1232.reading: At the word 'army' the whole host rises without a gap, like two seas surging unchecked, and the work of war spreads on every side.
1232.event: The two armies rise and spread for battle.

1233.reading: Cloud meets cloud and dark sea meets sea as chariot with chariot and horse with horse crowd into the fight.
1233.event: Chariots and cavalry of the two sides close with each other.

1234.reading: Spear-bearing elephants and swarms of archers clash like mountains against mountains, the elephants bent on killing.
1234.nuance: The Tamil of this verse has broken word division and one line was repaired in the core file; the sense of lines 1 and 2 is held loosely.
1234.event: Elephants and bowmen meet in battle.

1235.reading: Elephants' banners and horses leap over crowded elephants, kings' crowns and the clouds, the whole field heaving.
1235.event: Horses leap over fallen elephants and crowns in the press.

1236.reading: Chariot wheels crush heads, rolling them aside, and the fighters, dazed, cannot tell which way the chariot comes.
1236.event: Chariot wheels crush heads and confuse the warriors.

1237.reading: Maddened elephants roam among the crowded horses and chariots, tearing up and breaking the foe's arms and weapons.
1237.event: Rutting elephants move through the enemy ranks.

1238.reading: Warriors with fire in their eyes fall like fish when swords strike, as thunder-bright blades flash against thunder.
1238.event: Fighters are struck down by sword blows.

1239.reading: Arrows set on the long bowstrings stand up like fish-baited hooks drawn taut, sharpened and flashing.
1239.event: Bowmen draw arrows to the string.

1240.reading: A bow named for the fire-eyed god pours a shower of blazing arrows, and the red flesh of the Vidyadharas swells into a flood.
1240.nuance: The archer is not named; the bow's name is unclear in the printed text.
1240.event: A fire-named bow rains arrows on the Vidyadharas and a river of blood forms.

1241.reading: The young king of the southern hills, wanting a bow to match the Vidyadhara golden mountain, rises like a mountain of Kama and joins battle.
1241.nuance: The identification of the young king rests on the story so far, and the compound in line 2 is obscure.
1241.event: The southern young king attacks the Vidyadhara host.

1242.reading: Vidyadharas with blazing swords and bows, arms like great mountains, appear before the youth as bright as Kama.
1242.event: The Vidyadharas press on the hero.

1243.reading: The Vidyadharas' arrows fly, the bows spit them out, and the quarters fill with darkness while the foes draw near.
1243.event: The Vidyadharas shoot at the hero until the sky goes dark.

1244.reading: The quiver sits at the hand, the bow stands, and the arrow runs in the time it takes to look: a picture of an archer too quick to see.
1244.nuance: Pure description of speed in shooting; no event is told and the subject is not named.

1245.reading: One arrow is loosed and becomes a thousand, uncountable, and they spread over the earth until they fill it.
1245.event: The hero's shooting multiplies one arrow into a thousand.

1246.reading: The arrows rise to the sky and strike the Vidyadharas in the eyes, the quarters go black, and they fall to the ground bewildered.
1246.event: The hero's arrows blind the Vidyadharas, who fall to the ground.

1247.reading: In the darkness the Vidyadharas puzzle, fear, hide and tumble, and break under arrows, some rolling on the ground.
1247.event: The Vidyadharas are routed in the dark.

1248.reading: The broken army scatters like a mountain collapsing, and the warriors who pound the foe like cobras struck go stumbling away.
1248.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 compare the pursuers to a cobra stirred by a touch; whether the comparison is for the pursuing heroes or the fleeing troops is not fixed.

1249.reading: Arrow-struck elephants scream, hold up their tails and stream water, and run with ears folded back.

1250.reading: Drums are split and crowns submerged, royal power lies low, chariots clatter and horses stumble, and a river of blood runs down.
1250.nuance: 'Crowns sunk' (முடிகள் மூழ்கின) and 'kings subdued' (அரசுகள் அவிந்தன) are the narrator's summary of a whole host breaking.
1250.event: The rival army's drums, crowns and chariots are overthrown in a river of blood.

1251.reading: The army has broken today like a sea beaten by the wind, says the staff-bearer, bowing to the proud king whose sea-like host has failed.
1251.nuance: The identity of the proud king (taken as the rival king Acuvakanthan) and of the staff-bearer rests on the story so far.
1251.event: The staff-bearer bows to the proud king and reports the breaking of the army.

1252.reading: The speaker says that, as learning and subtle hearing bring many fruits, so war brings many fruits and fame; yet the foe has taken victory by the spear, and our men have taken fear in their feet.
1252.nuance: The first two lines are a comparison and the grammar is hard to fix; the second half plainly reports the rout.

claims.claim: weapons win the same kind of fame that learning wins

1253.reading: The earth's kings, who came to fight alongside us and have now turned their backs, grin with long teeth like rolled fire, asking what is left that is hard.
1253.nuance: Whether these kings are the rival's allies or the victor's side is not clear from the verse.
1253.event: The allied kings laugh at the retreat of those who came to fight.

1254.reading: Proud kings who did not break at the sea of arrows did break at the bow in the sun-like hand, and, ashamed of their own littleness, did not retreat to their own mountain.
1254.event: The proud kings break before the hero's bow and are too ashamed to flee home.

claims.claim: a proud king prefers shame at his own weakness to returning to his mountain refuge

1255.reading: The mountain-shouldered king laughs: if one man with one bow and two arms has broken the army today, then war is good for our men.
1255.nuance: The king's laugh takes the report of defeat as a boast, as the Kural's warrior laughs at his own wound.
1255.event: The rival king laughs at the report of his broken army.

links.note: 1243 has the Vidyadharas' arrows darken the sky; 1246 has the hero's arrows rise, strike their eyes and darken it again.
links.teaches: The darkness changes sides inside four verses, so the same arrow-shadow that shields the attackers blinds them.

links.note: 1251 reports the broken army to the proud king; 1255 gives the king's answer, a laugh.
links.teaches: The king's laugh meets news of ruin with a boast, making defeat into proof of the foe's single-handed skill.

links.note: The Kural names the army that does not collapse; 1250 shows drums split, crowns sunk and chariots overturned in a collapsing army.
links.teaches: A rule that an army must not collapse is tested against the detail of what a collapse looks like in a field.

gains.a: A standard to measure the broken host against, so its rout reads as failure of what an army must be.
gains.b: A worked case of collapse, which the definition names but never pictures.

links.note: The Kural calls an eye that blinks at a flung spear flight; 1247 has whole ranks blind with arrows, puzzled, hiding and falling.
links.teaches: The Kural counts flinching as flight, but 1247 shows troops struck blind by a dark of arrows, where fear and confusion are not the same.

gains.a: A name for the fear it shows, making the rout a failing of courage and not only of fortune.
gains.b: A case where the eye cannot see, which tests whether blinking is always cowardice.

links.note: The Kural's warrior laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body; 1255 has a king laugh at his army's rout.
links.teaches: The laugh of a warrior pulling a spear from his body is a private triumph, while a king's laugh at a lost army is a boast over others' loss.

gains.a: A measure of what the king's laugh costs against the warrior who laughs at his own wound.
gains.b: A contrasting laugh, from a leader and not the wounded fighter, which tests how far the Kural's praise reaches.

links.note: 1233 sets cloud against cloud and sea against sea as two hosts meet; Purananuru 17 sees the Chera king's host as an army like the sea.
links.teaches: The sea-army that praise sets at rest as a king's glory here meets another sea, and the figure turns from praise into clash.

gains.a: A source for the sea-army figure, here shown as one sea among two.
gains.b: A second sea set against the king's, so the image of an unopposed host meets its match.

source_issues: Verse 1234 had a line repaired for a stray pulli.
Verses 1231 to 1255 have broken word division in many places and several readings are held loosely.
The speaker and referent of 1251 to 1255 are not named beyond their epithets; they are read from the story so far.
